newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lower Russian T-bill yield seen reaction to rating.
newsitem.headline: Lower Russian T-bill yield seen reaction to rating.

text.p: A cut in the effective yield for non-residents in Russia's Treasury bill market reflects its newly-acquired credit rating and the return should still be enough to attract foreign investors, analysts said on Tuesday.
The central bank said on Monday that the effective dollar yield for non-resident investors in government securities would be cut to 16 percent from 19 percent from October 16.
The cut was announced as rating agencies unveiled generally better than expected credit ratings for Russian debt, opening the way for Russia to issue its debut Eurobond later this year.
"It is obvious that 19 percent is too much for a country which has credit ratings," said Oleg Surkov, senior manager, capital markets, at ICFI.

Foreign investors can command much higher yields in the secondary market, as 19 percent is the minimum available on a three-month bill held to maturity, and Surkov said the cut would not influence non-residents.
Six-month bills are yielding about 53 percent annually for domestic investors, having hit 80 percent two weeks ago.
Analysts say T-bills are still attractive compared with dollar-denominated MinFin bonds, which yield between 11.5 and 13.5 percent, and compared with paper in other emerging markets.
But the government has said it wants to cut yields on state securities to bring down interest rates. It also wants to shift to instruments of longer maturity and raise foreign borrowing.
Nima Tayebi, head of fixed income research at Renaissance Capital, said the cut partly reflected the rating, and the expectation that it would bring in more foreign investment.
"It is essentially capitalising on this improvement in the perception of the rating," he said.
Yields rose last month, partly on concern over the health of Presient Boris Yeltsin, who is awaiting heart surgery.

"With the ratings that have come out and the Eurobond on schedule, people are very much dismissing the health issue to the back of their minds and I think in the next few days that there is going to be significant foreign interest," Tayebi said.

Since August, non-residents have been able to open special "S" accounts at designated Russian banks to buy roubles and trade in the government securities market. The central bank said last month that only a few of the designated banks were active.
Non-residents can repatriate unlimited amounts of the rouble proceeds by buying foreign currency, using forwards or options with a term of at least three months.

The central bank regulates the effective dollar yield by requiring the Russian banks carrying out the forward deals to offset a certain proportion of these deals with the central bank at special rates set by the central bank.
Andrei Yashchenko, fixed income analyst at United City Bank, said the T-bill yield also reflected counterparty risk.
"The assignment of the ratings means the current GKO yields are above what the Eurobond will yield but...the dollar yields of GKOs should include sufficient premiums for the credit risks," he said.

The 1997 draft budget, which goes to parliament for a first reading on Friday, foresees some 45 trillion roubles ($8.3 billion) of the 90 trillion deficit covered by T-bills and government bonds. Russia also plans to issue $1.3 billion in Eurobonds in 1997.

The International Monetary Fund, which agreed a $10 billion, three-year loan programme with Russia earlier this year, wants Russia to increase foreign access to its securities market to lower interest rates.
Russian officials have said access will be gradually eased but that they want to be able to control the flow of money into and out of the market.
